title: IndiGo Held Liable for Denying Boarding After It Rescheduled the Flight, Rules Delhi Consumer Commission
meta_description: Delhi consumer commission finds IndiGo liable for marking a passenger a no-show after rescheduling his flight, rejecting its Carriage defence.
court: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I (North District), Delhi
bench: President and Members, District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I (North District), Delhi
case_name: Deyzeel Aggarwal v. InterGlobe Aviation Ltd.
citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I (North District), Delhi, order reported 16 September 2026
body: A passenger who shows up before his rescheduled departure time should not be the one penalised when the airline's own records fail to catch up with its own reschedule. A Delhi consumer commission has said exactly that to IndiGo, finding the airline liable after it marked a traveller a no-show despite his having turned up ahead of the delayed departure it had itself notified him of.

The complainant, Deyzeel Aggarwal, was booked on a Delhi to Bengaluru flight. IndiGo sent him an SMS and an email informing him that the flight had been delayed for operational reasons and moved to a 4:00 PM departure. Relying on that communication, Aggarwal reached the airport counter at 2:45 PM, well ahead of the newly notified departure time. IndiGo nonetheless treated him as a No Show, citing his failure to meet mandatory check-in timelines, and refused to let him board.

Delhi's District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I, North District, found that conduct amounted to both deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice. An airline that sends a passenger a reschedule notice cannot then fall back on check-in deadlines calculated from the original, superseded schedule to deny him boarding when he arrives in good time against the schedule it actually communicated to him.

IndiGo's defence leaned heavily on its Conditions of Carriage, the standard-form terms every air passenger accepts on booking, which the airline argued limited its liability for exactly this kind of dispute. The Commission was not persuaded. It held that contractual limitation clauses in an airline's Conditions of Carriage cannot operate as a complete defence against the statutory remedies a consumer is entitled to under the Consumer Protection Act. A carrier's standard terms, in other words, can shape the relationship between airline and passenger, but they cannot be used to override rights Parliament has given consumers independently of that contract.

That holding matters well beyond this one passenger's Rs 12,713 ticket. Airlines across India routinely point to their Conditions of Carriage whenever a deficiency complaint reaches a consumer forum, treating the contract as close to a complete shield. This ruling tells consumer commissions, and airlines, that such clauses get weighed against the statutory scheme rather than treated as automatically conclusive.

On relief, the Commission ordered IndiGo to refund the ticket fare of Rs 12,713 with 9 per cent interest, pay Rs 50,000 for the mental agony the denied boarding caused, and bear Rs 5,000 in litigation costs. Modest as the refund amount is on its own, the compensation for mental agony and the costs award reflect the Commission's view that being wrongly denied boarding, after doing everything the airline's own notice asked of him, is a real harm deserving more than a token remedy.

For passengers caught in similar disputes, the ruling offers a practical template: keep the SMS or email notifying a schedule change, note the time of arrival at the counter relative to that notified schedule, and be ready to argue that the airline's own communication, not its boilerplate Conditions of Carriage, governs what counted as timely check-in on the day. For airlines, the message is equally direct: internal check-in systems need to track an actual rescheduled departure time, not an original one the airline itself has already discarded, or they risk facing exactly this kind of liability again. The decision also fits a pattern that other consumer forums across the country have been building for several years now, where airlines are increasingly held to the substance of the communication they actually send a passenger rather than to a static rulebook buried deep in their website's terms and conditions. Commissions in other cities have taken a similar line in disputes over missed connections and overbooked flights, treating the airline's operational conduct on the day as the real measure of deficiency, with the Conditions of Carriage acting as a backdrop rather than a trump card. A point practitioners should flag for clients is how modest the direct financial loss was here against the relief actually awarded. The refunded fare of Rs 12,713 is dwarfed by the Rs 50,000 awarded for mental agony, a ratio that reflects how consumer commissions increasingly treat the inconvenience and distress of being wrongly denied boarding as the real harm in such disputes, separate from and larger than the bare monetary loss on the ticket itself. Complainants preparing similar cases should plead and evidence that distress carefully rather than focus solely on recovering the fare. Airlines operating in India would be wise to treat this ruling as a prompt to audit how their reservation and check-in systems handle a rescheduled departure once that reschedule has actually been communicated to the passenger. A system that still measures check-in compliance against an old departure time, after telling the passenger a new one applies, is building exactly the kind of liability this Commission was willing to impose, and there is little reason to expect other consumer forums across India to take a different view on the same basic facts.
why_it_matters: Airlines cannot rely on Conditions of Carriage as a blanket defence when a passenger follows the airline's own reschedule notice and is still denied boarding for allegedly missing check-in deadlines calculated against the original, superseded schedule. The ruling gives consumer forums a basis to look past standard-form airline contracts and apply statutory consumer protection remedies directly, strengthening the hand of passengers caught out by airlines' internal scheduling or communication failures.
card_summary: Delhi consumer commission holds IndiGo liable for marking a passenger a no-show after he arrived ahead of the delayed departure time the airline itself had texted him, rejecting its Conditions of Carriage defence.
card_tip: If an airline reschedules your flight and still denies boarding, keep that SMS or email; a commission can treat it as overriding the Conditions of Carriage on check-in timing.
verification_notes: Confirmed via LiveLaw's report (16 September 2026), SupremeToday.ai's matching report of the same date, and Indialaw.in's commentary, all describing the same facts: the complainant's reschedule SMS/email, arrival at 2:45 PM against a 4:00 PM notified departure, the No Show designation, the Commission's finding of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, its rejection of Conditions of Carriage as a complete defence, and the relief of a Rs 12,713 refund with 9% interest, Rs 50,000 for mental agony and Rs 5,000 in costs. The complainant's name, Deyzeel Aggarwal, and the respondent, InterGlobe Aviation Ltd. (IndiGo), are both reported, though no formal case number was available in any secondary report consulted; the case caption used here follows directly from the reported party names.
